To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the gene expression profile in mouse blood following neutron radiation is characterized by down-regulation of genes involved in nucleotide metabolism, up-regulation of genes related to lipid metabolism, and a bi-directional response for genes involved in cell cycle regulation, with downregulation at day 1 followed by upregulation at day seven after exposure.
neutrons result in more downregulated genes, and that the cell cycle genes that are downregulated at day one after exposure are distinct from the cell-cycle genes that are upregulated at day seven.
neutron radiation results mostly in downregulation of gene expression, while x-rays cause a mixed response, with upregulated as well as downregulated genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of radiation biodosimetry tools for use in the aftermath of a nuclear detonation.
the identification of genes that may be used to differentiate the effects of neutron from x-ray radiation in the context of a radiological incident.
the identification of gene expression changes that occur in the blood of exposed mice following neutron or x-ray exposures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
neutrons and x-rays have a distinct gene expression signature in mouse blood cells.
neutrons and x-rays cause a distinct gene expression response in the blood.

neutron radiation induces a different gene expression profile than that induced by x-rays, with a greater number of downregulated genes, and that this profile is more persistent than that induced by the same dose of x-rays.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neutrons and x-rays have different gene expression responses in the mouse blood.
neutron radiation causes more damage to the cell cycle and nucleic acid metabolism pathways, and that these changes are more persistent than in response to x-ray radiation.
neutron exposure resulted in more severe damage to the blood, and that this damage was more persistent than that seen with x-rays.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gene expression profile is a function of the dose, type of radiation, and time since exposure.
the gene expression response to neutrons is distinct from that of x-rays, and that the gene expression profiles are not consistent across the time points studied.
the biological effects of neutron radiation can be distinguished from x-ray radiation, and the gene expression profile can be used to distinguish the two radiation types.
